---
title: "Validation status"
---

This chapter records what has and has not been run, so nobody has to guess.
It is written by hand after each test round and contains only observed facts.
Nothing here is a benchmark or a biological result.

## Automated tests (no real tools)

`pytest -q tests` runs on any machine with Snakemake 8.27.1, pandas, numpy,
plotly and pytest (no conda, no STAR). It covers:

- Snakemake **dry runs** against tiny placeholder inputs (full, processing-only,
  analysis-only, trimming, per-sample tracks, GSEA branch, bad configs rejected,
  the FASTA/GTF chromosome-name check, and the spike-in module switched off,
  on with each size-factor method, and on with an index that lacks the
  spike-in contigs);
- a regression test that really runs the sample-table rule and checks that editing
  the samplesheet regenerates it (see the bug found below);
- the Python scripts (gene table, count matrix, scale factors, QC summary, QC
  report, results explorer, stranded signal page) on **synthetic** inputs, and the
  results explorer's controls driven in headless Chrome on synthetic data;
- the spike-in scripts (`tests/test_spike_in.py`): the combined host + spike-in
  reference (prefixing, the `gene` lines added for an exon-only spike-in GTF, the
  refusal of a host contig that already carries the prefix), spike-in pair counts,
  track factors on the spike-in and host bases, per-sample factors, DESeq2 size
  factors with the `total` method and the error for a sample with zero spike-in
  pairs. The fixtures `tests/dryrun/spike.fa` and `spike.gtf` mirror the layout of
  ERCC92 (exon-only, `gene_id` equal to the contig name); the real ERCC files are
  not in the repository;
- the pure-logic parts of the R scripts (ranking, classification, design checks);
- that the rule-graph diagrams in the docs are current.

At the last full run, 105 tests passed with R available, and 92 passed with 13
skipped (the R-script tests) on Python 3.11 without R, which is how the GitHub CI
runner behaves. That count predates the stranded-signal and spike-in tests;
those tests were later run and passed on the cluster. These tests show the workflow parses and that the scripts behave on
made-up inputs. They do **not** show that STAR, DESeq2 or any other tool gives good
results.

## Real-data test: mouse (two rounds, one cluster)

**What was run.** Public TT-seq data from GEO series GSE260914 (mouse ESC, ZFP143
dTAG degron). Only the **first 3 million read pairs** of each run were used (44 nt
reads), so these are the first reads in each file, not a random sample. Round 1 used
DMSO and 2 h (two replicates each); round 2 added 6 h and 24 h, giving 8 samples and
three contrasts against DMSO. The reference was mm10 with GENCODE vM25. Gene sets
for GSEA were the MSigDB mouse Hallmark, GO:BP and Reactome collections (release
2023.2). The workflow ran on a SLURM cluster (Case Western's Pioneer, `pioneer`
profile) with per-rule conda environments on linux-64.

**What was found and fixed along the way.**

- MultiQC 1.14 failed at import (`No module named 'pkg_resources'`) because the
  newest setuptools no longer provides it; `envs/ttpipe_multiqc.yml` now pins
  `setuptools<70`.
- Environment builds failed twice with `Disk quota exceeded` because conda's package
  cache and Snakemake's cache live under the user's home directory. This is a site
  issue, not a pipeline one; see [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) and
  [Cluster](cluster.qmd).
- **A real bug in TTpipe**: after adding samples to an existing output folder, DESeq2
  failed with "sample names differ between the count matrix and the sample table".
  The sample-table rule did not list the samplesheet as an input, so Snakemake kept
  a stale table. The samplesheet is now an input of `sample_table`, `qc_summary` and
  `qc_report`, and a regression test fails on the old rule and passes on the fix.
  Starting from an empty output folder would never have shown it.
- Once fixed, only the 18 jobs that had not finished were run; the finished
  alignments were not repeated.

**What worked on real data.** All 117 planned jobs of the 8-sample workflow
completed (across three submissions, because of the two failures above). All six
conda environments solved on linux-64, including STAR 2.7.9a with samtools 1.12 and
Picard 2.25.6 in one environment. The QC report's parsers read the real STAR
`Log.final.out`, Picard metrics, STAR `ReadsPerGene` and HTSeq counts without errors.
MultiQC found the FastQC, STAR and Picard reports. DESeq2 ran for three contrasts,
fgsea for three collections x three contrasts (nine result tables), the Sankey drew a
three-axis parallel set (2 h, 6 h, 24 h) and the PCA was produced.

**Observed values on this subset** (illustrative of the report, not a quality
statement about the data):

| Quantity | Observed range over 8 samples |
|---|---|
| Uniquely mapped (STAR) | 62.3 to 68.9 % |
| Multi-mapped | 7.2 to 8.7 % |
| Unmapped, too short | 22.8 to 29.2 % |
| Duplication (Picard) | 17.7 to 32.1 % |
| Reads on the gene strand (HTSeq, `sum` counting) | 86.7 to 88.9 % |
| rRNA genes, % of counted reads | 7.2 to 12.9 % |
| Replicate correlation (Pearson, log2 CPM), per condition | 0.943 to 0.960 |
| Computed bigWig scale factors (DMSO, 2 h, 6 h, 24 h) | 1.216, 1.083, 1.043, 1 |

Against the default thresholds in the config, the strand and rRNA values and some
replicate correlations fall in the **warn** range. The thresholds' `fail` values are
TTpipe defaults, not literature values.

DESeq2 (each contrast vs DMSO, alpha 0.01) called, with the number of genes with a
non-missing adjusted p-value in brackets: 2 h, 6 up and 43 down (11,337); 6 h, 17 up
and 58 down (11,337); 24 h, 25 up and 114 down (12,638). With two replicates and a
3-million-pair subset this says nothing about the biology. fgsea (adjusted p < 0.05)
reported, for 2 h, 6 h and 24 h respectively: Hallmark 15, 9 and 11 of 50 sets; GO:BP
216, 309 and 296 of 7,726; Reactome 52, 24 and 21 of 1,250. These are counts of sets
that passed a threshold, not an interpretation, and fgsea was never compared with the
Java GSEA tool.

**Results explorer.** The explorer rule ran as a real Snakemake job on the cluster, in
its conda environment, and wrote the page from the real tables (13,419 genes, three
contrasts, GSEA and normalized counts; 11.4 MB). The scripted interaction checks built
into the page (contrast and plot switching, live cut-offs, biotype filter, gene search,
count plot, table sorting and filtering, CSV text, GSEA tab) all passed in headless
Chrome, with zero failures, on both a locally built copy and the cluster-built file.
Its up/down counts for the 2 h contrast (6 up, 43 down) match the pipeline's own
`deg_summary.tsv`.

**Measured resource use** (from Snakemake benchmark files in the first round):
STAR alignment used about 25.7 GB of memory (depends on the genome, not the number
of reads) and the STAR index build about 28.9 GB and 36 minutes. Every other rule
used roughly 1.2 GB or less. Run times are for 3-million-pair inputs only and do not
extrapolate to full-depth samples; the per-rule values in the profiles remain
starting values.

**Stranded signal page (a later round on the same data).** The `stranded_signal`
rule ran as a real cluster job on the 8-sample mouse output and took about 4
minutes. It counted 13,419 expressed genes (count >= 10 in at least 2 samples). The
protein-coding metagene used 11,348 genes (11,345 in the TSS view, 11,294 in the
gene-body view); the strand table listed 13,837 genes with at least 50 reads; all 19
locus tracks were found; the page was 6.0 MB. Known genes came out on the expected
strand: Gapdh (minus strand) had 355 to 391 reads on the reverse strand against 6 to
13 on the forward, and Zfp143 (plus strand) 200 to 212 on the forward against 1 to 3
on the reverse, about 97 to 99 % sense.

What was found and fixed: the **lncRNA metagene group was empty** on this data.
GENCODE vM25 still labels mouse long non-coding genes with the older types
(`lincRNA`, `antisense` and so on) rather than `lncRNA`. The group now also takes
those older GENCODE types and its label lists the ones it included (see
[Configuration](configuration.qmd)). After the fix the lncRNA metagene used 1,389
genes (1,389 in the TSS view, 1,363 in the gene-body view). The first attempt of the
job failed for an unrelated reason, a conda environment that was still being written
by an overlapping build (see [Operational problems](#operational-problems) below);
the rerun was fine.

## Real-data test: human with ERCC spike-in (processing only)

**What was run.** Public chrTT-seq data from GEO series GSE218726 (human MCF-7
cells): 10 samples of chromatin-associated ("Assoc") and chromatin-released
("Released") nascent RNA after a 4sU pulse-chase of 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes, one
sample per condition (no replicates). Only the **first 2 million read pairs** of each
run were used (75 nt reads). The libraries are TruSeq Stranded mRNA (dUTP), and
`strandedness: dUTP` was confirmed by the strand check below. Per GEO, the samples
contain three 4sU-labeled and three unlabeled ERCC spike-in RNAs.

The reference was the GRCh38 primary assembly (GENCODE release 44 FASTA, MD5
checked) with the GENCODE v44 annotation, plus ERCC92 (92 contigs, exon-only GTF).
STAR 2.7.9a, `sjdb_overhang: 100`. The config had `run_processing: true`,
`run_analysis: false`, `spike_in.enabled: true`, `normalize: ['tracks']` and
`use_contigs: []` (all spike-in contigs). The run used the `pioneer` profile on SLURM.

**What worked on real data.** The combined human + ERCC STAR index was built by a
standalone job with the same command as the pipeline's `star_index` rule. The
workflow itself, 170 jobs, all completed in about 34 minutes of wall time, and wrote
the stranded signal page, the QC report and the MultiQC report. Known genes came out
on the expected strand, so the dUTP handling is right on human: GAPDH (plus strand)
had 23, 48 and 36 forward against 2, 1 and 5 reverse counts in the first three
samples; ACTB (minus strand) had 1, 3 and 7 forward against 52, 107 and 105 reverse.
The spike-in genes stayed out of the host matrices: `counts_deseq2.txt` contains no
`spike_` gene id, and `counts_spike.txt` has 92 rows, 6 of them non-zero.

**Observed values on this subset** (illustrative of the report, not a quality
statement about the data):

| Quantity | Observed range over 10 samples |
|---|---|
| Uniquely mapped (STAR) | 26.3 to 52.8 % |
| Multi-mapped | 44.6 to 71.2 % |
| Unmapped, too short | 2.5 to 6.6 % |
| Final pairs, % of input | 16.1 to 39.3 % |
| Duplication (Picard) | 19.5 to 38.6 % |
| Reads on the gene strand (HTSeq) | 86.3 to 90.7 % |
| rRNA genes, % of counted reads | 0.3 to 19.9 % |
| Host pairs per sample (final BAM) | 322,245 to 785,168 |
| Spike-in pairs per sample (final BAM) | 30 to 89 (0.006 to 0.023 %) |
| Track scale factors (spike-in basis) | 1.00 (Released_10min, 89 pairs) to 2.97 (Assoc_20min, 30 pairs) |

High multi-mapping is expected for chromatin-associated RNA with rRNA and repeat
content; nothing more is read into it here. The factor arithmetic checks out by hand
(89 / 30 = 2.97).

**The spike-in factors are a test of the mechanics, not usable normalization.**
With 30 to 89 spike-in pairs per sample, counting (Poisson) noise alone is about 10
to 18 %. Full-depth data would have roughly 10 to 20 times more spike-in reads.

**Which spike-ins to use.** TT-seq kits often add a few 4sU-labeled and a few
unlabeled spike-in RNAs. Only the labeled ones go through the 4sU purification, so
`use_contigs` should list the labeled ones. In this data exactly six ERCC contigs
received reads (ERCC-00002, ERCC-00043, ERCC-00092, ERCC-00136, ERCC-00145,
ERCC-00170). Which three of them were labeled was **not** determined (it should be in
the methods of the paper, PMID 37857083); this test used all six.

**Measured resource use** (Snakemake benchmark files and SLURM accounting): the
human + ERCC STAR index build took 34 minutes on 16 threads with a peak of 62.5 GB
(65,525,800 KB MaxRSS), against about 29 GB for mouse; the `pioneer` profile's
`star_index` memory was raised from 48000 to 72000 MB because of it. STAR alignment
peaked at about 29.0 GB per sample. Every other rule used 2.5 GB or less
(`stranded_signal` 2.4 GB, `mark_duplicates` about 1.4 GB). As with mouse, the run
times are for subsampled inputs only.

## Operational problems found {#operational-problems}

These came up during the later rounds. None is a bug in the analysis; each is
described with its fix in [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) or
[Cluster](cluster.qmd).

- **Overlapping conda builds broke environments.** Building environments on the
  login node was killed partway, and two builds (or a build and a running job) used
  the same `.snakemake/conda` folder and package cache at once. The result was
  environments with missing standard-library files, which failed with
  `No module named '__future__'`, `Could not find platform independent libraries`
  or `init_fs_encoding: failed to get the Python codec`. Deleting the broken
  environment folders and the package cache and rebuilding once fixed it. On
  Pioneer the compute nodes have internet access, so all 7 environments were then
  built in one SLURM job (69 minutes, 8 cores, 32 GB).
- **The placeholder account fails the launcher, not the dry run.** With
  `slurm_account: <your-slurm-account>` still in the profile, `bash TTpipe.sh -n`
  passes, but the submitted launcher fails within a minute with
  `Failed to evaluate resources value '<your-slurm-account>'`.
- **`reference_condition` is checked even with `run_analysis: false`.** The shipped
  config says `'DMSO'`, so a samplesheet without a DMSO condition stops at startup
  even for a processing-only run. Setting `reference_condition` to one of the
  samplesheet's conditions avoids it. This is not changed in the code.

## What has not been run

- **Full-depth data.** The mouse samples have roughly 30 to 48 million pairs; no
  sample, mouse or human, was run at full depth.
- **The explorer in browsers other than Chrome**, with real mouse hover, or an actual CSV
  file download (the CSV text is generated and checked, but the download itself was not triggered).
- **Optional switches** on real data: `trim: true` (fastp), `strandedness: forward`,
  `count_strand: sense`, `sample_tracks: true`, `analysis_counts`.
- **Analysis on human.** Human (GRCh38, GENCODE v44) was run for processing only;
  DESeq2, fgsea, the Sankey and the results explorer have not been run on human data.
- **Other organisms.** Only mouse and human have been run.
- **Other clusters and platforms.** Only one cluster was used. STAR 2.7.9a, samtools
  1.12 and HTSeq 0.13.5 have no osx-arm64 builds, so a laptop run on Apple silicon was not attempted.
- **Parts of the spike-in module.** The module is experimental and off by default.
  Spike-in counting and track factors were run on real data (above), but DESeq2 with
  spike-in size factors (`normalize` containing `deseq2`), `size_factor_method:
  'genes'`, and spike-in data with replicates have not been. The QC report does not
  show spike-in numbers yet (they are in `spike/spike_counts.tsv`), and `min_pairs`
  is not used.
- **Labeled-vs-total, eRNA discovery, tracks panel and rate analyses** do not exist
  in this version.

## Repeating the real-data tests

Mouse:

1. List the TT-seq runs of GSE260914 with the ENA read-only API (filter
   `study_alias="GSE260914"`; select runs whose title starts with `TTseq_`).
2. Subsample reads, for example with `gunzip -c ... | head -n 12000000 | gzip`
   per mate for 3 million pairs, and check that the line counts and read IDs of mate
   1 and mate 2 match (a dropped connection can truncate a stream).
3. Use a FASTA and GTF with the same chromosome naming, set `build_star_index: true`
   and `sjdb_overhang` to read length minus 1.
4. Build the environments on a node with internet
   (`bash TTpipe.sh --conda-create-envs-only`), then submit `TTpipe.sh`.

Human with ERCC spike-in: list the runs of GSE218726 with the ENA read-only API (`study_alias="GSE218726"`), take the first
2 million pairs per mate (`head -n 8000000`), download the GENCODE release 44 GRCh38
primary-assembly FASTA and v44 annotation GTF plus ERCC92 (`ERCC92.fa`,
`ERCC92.gtf`), and set `spike_in.enabled: true` with `fasta` and `gtf` pointing at
the ERCC files, `build_star_index: true` with a new `star_index` folder,
`sjdb_overhang: 100`, `run_analysis: false` and `reference_condition` set to one of
your conditions. The index build peaked at 62.5 GB, so give `star_index` more than
that (the `pioneer` profile now asks for 72 GB).
